Let's take a closer look at discrete I/O modules.
Discrete I/O modules are also called digital I/O modules and include the relay and TTL types. Relay I/O modules require 12 to 24 volts for operation while TTL units operate on 5 volts.
Discrete I/O modules are used with on/off or open/closed types of input and output devices such as push button switches, relays, and indicator lights.
The basic circuitry is similar for both AC and DC units, but AC units often contain additional components for signal rectification.
The signal enters a detector and rectifier block within the input module's circuit. Detector & Rectifier

The signal is converted in the detector & rectifier block in order to drive a transmitter in the opto-isolator block. The opto-isolator block electrically isolates the processor from the input signals.
The signal passes from the opto-isolator block to the digital logic block where it is converted into a digital form that is acceptable to the CPU.
A discrete output module's circuit operates in a reverse fashion by taking the signal from the CPU, sending it to an opto-isolator, and converting it to an appropriate output signal.
I/O modules may contain strictly inputs, strictly outputs or both inputs and outputs.

Each I/O module is issued a unique address. The CPU uses this address to identify the location of the I/O module for proper ladder logic operation.
All addressing schemes contain these four basic elements. Any additional required information may vary.
BASIC ADDRESSING ELEMENTS
TYPE The type determines if an input or an output is used.
SLOT The slot number is the physical location of the I/O module. This may be a combination of the rack number and the slot number when using expansion racks.

WORD & BIT The word and bit are used to identify the actual connection in a particular I/O module. Discrete modules usually have only one word and each connection corresponds to a different bit. In analog modules, the bit address is usually not used.

DISCUSSION
Most processor modules contain three important parts.
NIDA MODEL 5050 PLC TRAINER - The CPU is located within the processor module.
The CPU is the brain of the PLC and it executes the user's ladder logic program.
Different microprocessors with different capabilities are available in order to meet the demands of the user.
The best microprocessor is chosen by determining anticipated needs such as amount of memory, number of I/O channels, and speed of operation.
Let's take a look at the memory in a PLC processor module..
The processor module's memory contains all programs and data necessary for PLC operation. Some portions are installed during manufacturing while others are accessible to the user.
Read Only Memory - Cannot be changed oce programmed
Random Access Memory - Easily changed, but contents lost with power loss
Electrically Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory

A memory map diagram illustrates the organization of the memory information within the processor module.
The memory map can be divided into a fixed section and a variable section with different memory types used for each.
The fixed section includes programs that do not change during normal operation such as the main program and the user's ladder logic program.
ROM, PROM, EPROM, EAROM, or EEPROM are the best memory types for the fixed memory section.
The variable section includes data that changes during normal operation such as I/O image tables and instructional data.
Only RAM or EEPROM memory types are used for the variable section.
The I/O image tables reserve a portion of memory for each input and each output from the I/O modules.

The amount of memory used for the I/O image tables depends on the inputs and outputs. Digital inputs/outputs may only require a single memory bit while analog inputs/outputs require an entire word (16 bits)...

The processor module operates in a cyclic pattern referred to as a scan cycle which includes an I/O scan and a program scan.
The processor starts by scanning all of the input connections and records their status in the input image table.
Next, the processor systematically evaluates each rung of the ladder logic program. The output image table and internal data bits are set accordingly.
Finally, the processor scans the output image table and energizes all of the proper outputs.
The processor repeats the scan cycle continually as long as the PLC is on or in the run mode.
The amount of time required to complete the scan cycle is called scan time.
Scan time is an important consideration when selecting or troubleshooting a PLC since the PLC loses control of the processes if the inputs change faster than the scan time.
Which part of the scan cycle energizes the outputs?
The input scan involves scanning all the input connections and recording their status in the input image table but does not energize the outputs.
TRY AGAIN!
The program scan involves systematically evaluating each rung of the ladder logic program. The output image table and internal data bits are set accordingly but the outputs are not energized.
